{{confuse|Generalized metric space}}
In [[mathematics]], the concept of a '''generalised metric''' is a generalisation of that of a [[metric space|metric]], in which the distance is not a [[real number]] but taken from an arbitrary [[ordered field]].

In general, when we define [[metric space]] the distance function is taken to be a real-valued [[function (mathematics)|function]]. The real numbers form an ordered field which is [[archimedean property|Archimedean]] and [[complete ordered field|order complete]]. These metric spaces have some nice properties like: in a metric space [[compactness]], [[sequential compactness]] and [[countable compactness]] are equivalent etc. These properties may not, however, hold so easily if the distance function is taken in an arbitrary ordered field, instead of in <math>\scriptstyle \R.</math>

==Preliminary definition==

Let <math>(F, +, \cdot, <)</math> be an arbitrary ordered field, and <math>M</math> a nonempty set; a function <math>d : M \times M \to F^+ \cup \{0\}</math> is called a metric on <math>M,</math> if the following conditions hold:

# <math>d(x, y) = 0</math> if and only if <math>x = y</math>;
# <math>d(x, y) = d(y, x)</math> (symmetry);
# <math>d(x, y) + d(y, z) \geq d(x, z)</math> (triangle inequality).

It is not difficult to verify that the open balls <math>B(x, \delta)\; := \{y \in M\; : d(x, y) < \delta\}</math> form a basis for a suitable topology, the latter called the  ''[[metric topology]]'' on <math>M,</math> with the metric in <math>F.</math>

Since <math>F</math> in its [[order topology]] is [[monotonically normal]], we would expect <math>M</math> to be at least [[Regular space|regular]].

==Further properties==

However, under [[axiom of choice]], every general metric is [[monotonically normal]], for, given <math>x \in G,</math> where <math>G</math> is open, there is an open ball <math>B(x, \delta)</math> such that <math>x \in B(x, \delta) \subseteq G.</math> Take <math>\mu(x, G) = B\left(x, \delta/2\right).</math> Verify the conditions for Monotone Normality.

The matter of wonder is that, even without choice, general metrics are [[monotonically normal]].

''proof''.

Case I: <math>F</math> is an [[Archimedean field]].

Now, if <math>x</math> in  <math>G, G</math> open, we may take <math>\mu(x, G) := B(x, 1/2n(x,G)),</math> where <math>n(x, G) := \min\{n \in \N : B(x, 1/n) \subseteq G\},</math> and the trick is done without choice.

Case II: <math>F</math> is a non-Archimedean field.

For given <math>x \in G</math> where <math>G</math> is open, consider the set
<math>A(x, G) := \{a \in F : \text{ for all } n \in \N, B(x, n \cdot a) \subseteq G\}.</math>

The set <math>A(x, G)</math> is non-empty. For, as <math>G</math> is open, there is an open ball <math>B(x, k)</math> within <math>G.</math> Now, as <math>F</math> is non-Archimdedean, <math>\N_F</math> is not bounded above, hence there is some <math>\xi \in F</math> such that for all <math>n \in \N,</math> <math>n \cdot 1 \leq \xi.</math> Putting <math>a = k \cdot (2 \xi)^{-1},</math> we see that <math>a</math> is in <math>A(x, G).</math>

Now define <math>\mu(x, G) = \bigcup\{B(x, a) : a \in A(x, G)\}.</math> We would show that with respect to this mu operator, the space is monotonically normal. Note that <math>\mu(x,G)\subseteq G.</math>

If <math>y</math> is not in <math>G</math> (open set containing <math>x</math>) and <math>x</math> is not in <math>H</math> (open set containing <math>y</math>), then we'd show that <math>\mu(x, G) \cap \mu(y, H)</math> is empty. If not, say <math>z</math> is in the intersection. Then
<math display=block>\exists a \in A(x, G) \colon d(x, z) < a;\;\;
\exists b \in A(y, H) \colon d(z, y) < b.</math>

From the above, we get that <math>d(x, y) \leq d(x, z) + d(z, y) < 2 \cdot \max\{a, b\},</math> which is impossible since this would imply that either <math>y</math> belongs to <math>\mu(x, G) \subseteq G</math> or <math>x</math> belongs to <math>\mu(y, H) \subseteq H.</math> 
This completes the proof.
